# Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.

Day 3, 16:00 · Gary Illyes, Search Relations · coverage: transcript, one-slide

Speaker from the author's recording label; same recording as How long does it take to..?, with no new introduction.

## Claims

- **[Stage]** Google said there is so much going on in Search that AI topics were covered across the event only where contextually important, and its closing message was to use AI but understand how it works so as to use it responsibly.
  <br><sub>`D3-C678` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google described AI as an umbrella of many technologies working together, one of which is machine learning: systems that learn from large amounts of data to make informed decisions.
  <br><sub>`D3-C679` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said machine learning is about 50 years old and that Google has been using it for 'probably 30 years', starting with statistical models that made the 'Did you mean' feature possible.
  <br><sub>`D3-C680` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C041](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Repeats [D1-C209](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Some of Google's search ranking features are plain machine learning models, because for some tasks simple machine learning models are more useful than large language models.
  <br><sub>`D3-C681` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google described large language models as deep learning on internet-scale data sets, trained so that the model has an internal vector space in which concepts are mapped by context.
  <br><sub>`D3-C682` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google distinguished predictive language models, whose primary job is to predict the next word or words in a text, from generative models that produce output from a prompt; next-word prediction is a guess, made with some accuracy, from the context given.
  <br><sub>`D3-C683` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Predictive language models have been used a lot in Search, and BERT is one: technically, in the purest sense, an LLM.
  <br><sub>`D3-C684` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide) · Extends [D1-C042](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *BERT, RankBrain and MUM*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said it thinks generative AI is extremely helpful to its users.
  <br><sub>`D3-C685` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Hallucinations can happen with any AI model, and with current training methods there is no way to get rid of them.
  <br><sub>`D3-C686` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Google Search's guidance on using generative AI content on your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/using-gen-ai-content) · Extends [D2-C462](../day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) · Used by `DEV-SPM-05`, the glossary term *Hallucination*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Adding grounding or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on top of a model reduces hallucinations but cannot eliminate them.
  <br><sub>`D3-C687` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Hallucination*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Generative models, including image diffusion models, make things up when they lack information or because of issues in their training.
  <br><sub>`D3-C688` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. - **[Stage]** Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines tell raters that any form of deception makes a page untrustworthy and earns it the lowest rating.
  <br><sub>`D3-C689` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Quality raters cannot give a site a penalty or a manual action; their ratings are converted into labels that Google uses to improve its algorithms.
  <br><sub>`D3-C690` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. - **[Stage]** Publishing AI output without checking it can indirectly harm a site's standing in Search, because deceptive content rated lowest by raters feeds the labels used to improve the algorithms.
  <br><sub>`D3-C691` · Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. - **[Stage]** Google sees fake online personas as a growing type of deception, for example a professional author bio whose headshot is an AI-generated image of a non-existent person, and pages doing this get the lowest rater rating.
